589.title: Rama in the rains
589.hook: Rama's monsoon poem, and why so many Hindu love songs ache
589.carry: viraha: longing is a kind of love
589.howItsDone: Viraha runs through Hindu devotion: the gopis' longing for Krishna in the Bhagavata Purana, Mirabai's songs, and countless bhajans sing of God as a beloved far away. Rama's monsoon description in the Kishkindha Kanda is often cited as an early model for later monsoon poems.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rains began, and chaturmas, the four holy months, with Rama waiting them out in chaturmas, the four holy months of rain.
screen: `CHATURMAS, THE FOUR HOLY MONTHS OF RAIN.`

segments.voice: The smell of wet earth after months of dust. The sky changing color in an afternoon. The whole land seeming to breathe out. Rama, waiting in the cave, describes the monsoon to Lakshmana, and it's some of the most famous nature writing in Sanskrit: a long, beautiful, aching poem. Rama sees all of that, and something else too.
screen: `THE SMELL OF WET EARTH.` → `FAMOUS NATURE WRITING.` → `RAMA SEES SOMETHING ELSE TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's how Valmiki's Rama sees it. The sky, he says, drank the waters of the sea through the sun's rays, carried them for nine months, and now is giving birth to rain. He sees clouds piled like mountains. He hears peacocks crying out and sees them dancing. Frogs wake and call. Rivers rush toward the sea. And the rain that is lovely for everyone is painful for him. Travelers are heading home, he says. Kings have stopped their campaigns. Everyone is going back to the one they love, and he can't. So every lovely thing he sees, he sees as someone apart from Sita. That feeling has a name in Sanskrit: viraha, love in separation. And here's why it matters far beyond this cave. Viraha became one of the great roads of Hindu devotion. In the Bhagavata Purana, when Krishna slips away from the cowherd women of Vrindavan, the gopis search the forest calling for him, and their song of longing is loved to this day. Saints like Mirabai sang to Krishna as a beloved who felt far away. Many teachers read it this way: in bhakti, longing for God isn't a failure of faith. It is love, still working, and the ache keeps the beloved close. That's why so many bhajans sound sad and sweet at once. Rama in the rains is the same mood from the other side. He doesn't stop loving because Sita is far. He looks harder. And it meets a life now: anyone missing a grandparent across an ocean, or someone gone. Hindu devotion doesn't say get over it. It says the missing is love.
screen: `THE SKY CARRIED THE SEA.` · `EVERYONE GOES HOME BUT RAMA.` · `VIRAHA: LOVE IN SEPARATION.` · `THE GOPIS LONG FOR KRISHNA.` · then, large: `LONGING IS A KIND OF LOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you miss. Breathe in and let yourself feel it, without fixing it. Breathe out. If you pray, say softly: Sita Ram, two names many Hindus chant together, the very two this story keeps apart. If you don't, simply say the name of the one you miss. Let the missing be love, held gently, then come back to the breath.
The rains. Rama's monsoon poem, and its mood, viraha: love in separation, the ache bhakti songs still sing.
Your line: viraha: longing is a kind of love. The missing keeps them close. See you tomorrow.

590.title: Hanuman's reminder
590.hook: a new king forgets his promise, and the four aims of a life
590.carry: kama is a real aim, but dharma comes first
590.howItsDone: Hindu teaching names four aims of life, the purusharthas: dharma, artha, kama and moksha. Autumn (sharad) opens the festival season, with Navaratri and Dussehra; in some regions Dussehra celebrates Rama's victory, in others Durga's.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rains, and viraha, Rama's longing for Sita: longing is a kind of love.

Down in Kishkindha, the new king is having a wonderful time, and Valmiki doesn't hide it. Sugriva has his kingdom back after years on the run. He has his wife Ruma back, and Tara is in the palace as his queen as well. He spends the season in comfort, feasting and drinking, with music in the halls. Up on the mountain, the rain falls on a cave. Then the rains end. The sky clears. And Sugriva hasn't noticed.
screen: `A WONDERFUL TIME IN KISHKINDHA.` → `MUSIC IN THE HALLS.` → `THE RAINS END, UNNOTICED.`

segments.voice: Hanuman notices. He goes to Sugriva first, before anyone gets angry. You have your kingdom, he says. Now it's time to help your friends. Rama helped you; it's your turn. Sugriva hears him, and orders the monkey armies gathered from every mountain and forest within fifteen days. Notice what Hanuman doesn't say. He doesn't tell Sugriva that enjoying himself was wicked, and Hindu teaching has a frame for why. It names four aims of a human life, the purusharthas: dharma, doing what's right; artha, wealth and security; kama, pleasure and love; and moksha, freedom. Kama is on the list. Music, food, love, a festival: in Hindu teaching these are real goods, not sins to be ashamed of. What the tradition asks about is order. Artha and kama are meant to be pursued inside dharma, not instead of it. As many teachers tell it, Sugriva's feast isn't the fault. The fault is that the feast pushed out a promise to a friend. Hanuman doesn't take the music away. He puts dharma back on top. Meanwhile the season turns. Autumn arrives, sharad: rivers clear, the sky is clean, the roads open. It's the season Hindus still fill with festivals, Navaratri's nine nights for the Goddess, full of dance, then Dussehra. Joy and devotion in the same week. Up on Prasravana, Rama sees the clear sky and hears no word. And it meets a life now: a Hindu doesn't have to choose between fun and faith. Dance at garba till midnight. Just keep your word in the morning.
screen: `HANUMAN'S REMINDER.` · `DHARMA, ARTHA, KAMA, MOKSHA.` · `KAMA, INSIDE DHARMA.` · `SHARAD: THE FESTIVAL SEASON.` · then, large: `KAMA IS REAL; DHARMA COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus offer food first, at the home shrine or silently, then eat it as prasad, a gift given back. Try it in the mind. Picture something you'll enjoy today: a meal, a song, time with a friend. Breathe in and offer it. Breathe out and receive it back as a gift. If you don't pray, pause and thank whoever made it possible. Enjoyment, held inside gratitude.
The rains. They end in a clear autumn sky, a feast that forgot a promise, and Hanuman's reminder.
Your line: kama is a real aim, but dharma comes first. Enjoy the feast; keep the promise. That's day five hundred ninety.

591.title: Rama's anger
591.hook: Rama's patience runs out, and the Gita's chain of anger
591.carry: krodha clouds memory: remember the friend
591.howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita (2.62–63) traces the chain from desire to anger to confusion and lost judgment, and Hindu teachers count anger (krodha) among the six inner enemies; storytellers use Rama's message to Sugriva to talk about anger that stays in bounds.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rains ended, and Hanuman's reminder: kama is a real aim, but dharma comes first.

No messenger. Not yesterday, not today. Rama looks down the mountain toward the city where his friend is enjoying a throne Rama won for him. He doesn't know about Hanuman's reminder or the orders that went out. All he sees is a clear road and a silent city. His patience, which has held through grief and rain, finally gives way. Valmiki lets us hear all of it.
screen: `NO MESSENGER.` → `A SILENT CITY BELOW.` → `PATIENCE GIVES WAY.`

segments.voice: Rama speaks to Lakshmana, first in grief, then in anger. The time we agreed on is here, he says, and Sugriva hasn't come. He thinks I'm a man without a kingdom, someone he can forget. So Rama gives Lakshmana a message to carry, and it isn't subtle: the path Vali took is not closed. Keep your word, or follow Vali. The word for what Sugriva let slip is samaya: an agreement, and also an appointed time. Then watch Lakshmana. Rama is angry; Lakshmana is angrier. He wants to go down and kill Sugriva today. So Rama, even while sending him, holds him back: don't kill him. Speak gently first. Remind him of the friendship. The Bhagavad Gita traces how anger runs, like a chain. Dwell on something and attachment grows; from attachment, desire; from desire, anger; from anger, confusion; from confusion, memory slips; and when memory goes, judgment goes with it. Hindu teachers count krodha, anger, among the six inner enemies. Many teachers read that lost memory as forgetting who someone is to you. Rama's anger is fair, and he still breaks the chain where it counts: he doesn't lose his memory of the friendship. He keeps his judgment, and keeps his brother on the reins. Lakshmana, left alone, might have run the chain to the end. It meets a life now in the angry text you're about to send. Rama's story doesn't pretend anger never comes. The Gita shows where it leads if you follow it: so stop before it steals your memory of who that person is to you. Lakshmana picks up his bow and walks down the mountain.
screen: `THE PATH VALI TOOK IS NOT CLOSED.` · `SPEAK GENTLY FIRST.` · `GITA 2.62–63: THE CHAIN OF ANGER.` · `RAMA KEEPS THE MEMORY.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Recall someone who let you down. Breathe in and feel the anger honestly, where it sits in your body. Breathe out slowly, and bring to mind one good thing that person has been to you: the kind of memory, many teachers say, that anger steals. If you pray, say Om shanti three times, the words that close so many Hindu prayers. If not, take three slow breaths out.
Lakshmana's warning. Rama's hard message, sent in anger that still remembers the friend.
Your line: krodha clouds memory: remember the friend. Rama was angry, and he still remembered. Until tomorrow.

592.title: Tara at the palace door
592.hook: a bowstring shakes the city, and Tara, one of five women Hindus remember
592.carry: panchakanya: Tara, the wise one, remembered daily
592.howItsDone: A traditional morning verse names five women, the panchakanya (Ahalya, Draupadi, Sita or Kunti, Tara and Mandodari), to be remembered daily; storytellers point to Tara here as a model of wise counsel.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's warning went down the mountain, from a Rama who was angry but remembered the friend.
screen: `THE PATH VALI TOOK IS NOT CLOSED.`

segments.voice: The monkeys at the gates of Kishkindha see Lakshmana coming and panic. He looks, Valmiki says, like the fire at the end of the world. They scramble up walls and into trees. Some grab boulders and branches, as if that would help. Young Angada goes to meet him and is sent running back inside with the message. Lakshmana walks straight through the city, past the fine houses and gardens, and at the palace he twangs his bowstring so loudly that the whole city shakes.
screen: `PANIC AT THE GATES.` → `LIKE THE FIRE AT THE END OF THE WORLD.` → `A BOWSTRING SHAKES THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Inside, Sugriva hears the bowstring, and the party is over. He's frightened, and at first can't think what he's done wrong; Hanuman has to tell him he let the time slip. He doesn't go out himself. He sends Tara. Not long ago she was a widow grieving before Rama. Now she walks out to meet his furious brother with complete poise. Why are you angry, prince? Sugriva has been careless, yes. Even great sages have been carried away, she says, and she names Vishvamitra, who spent years with the celestial dancer Ghritachi and thought it was a single day. Then she tells him what his anger was missing: orders have already gone out. Armies are on their way. Come in. Talk to him. Lakshmana listens, and his anger cools. Hindus have a way of remembering her. A traditional morning verse names five women, the panchakanya: Ahalya, Draupadi, Sita, in some versions Kunti, Tara and Mandodari, and says that remembering them each day washes away even great wrongs. Each has a hard story. Each lived through what the world would call ruin. And the tradition puts their names on the lips every morning. Many teachers read it as honoring wisdom and strength that outlast suffering. Tara is the one remembered for counsel. She warned Vali, and he didn't listen. This time somebody listens. It meets a life now: before your anger lands, there's often news you haven't heard. And the one who brings it may be the one who's been through the most.

593.title: Sugriva's apology
593.hook: an apology, armies covering the earth, and kshama
593.carry: kshama: forgiveness, patient as the earth
593.howItsDone: Kshama, forgiveness or forbearance, is listed among the divine qualities in the Bhagavad Gita (16.3); many Hindus begin the day with a short prayer asking Bhumi, the earth, to forgive the touch of their feet.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's warning met Tara, one of the panchakanya, and this time somebody listened.

Lakshmana walks into the inner palace. It's beautiful, full of gardens, music and fine things, and Valmiki describes it in detail, maybe so we'll feel how far Sugriva has drifted from a cave on a mountain. Sugriva is on his throne, in fine clothes and garlands, his queens around him. He sees Lakshmana and gets to his feet. Now the king of the monkeys has to face the brother of the man who made him king.
screen: `THE INNER PALACE.` → `SUGRIVA ON HIS THRONE.` → `HE GETS TO HIS FEET.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana speaks hard words. A king who takes help and doesn't keep his promise is ungrateful, he says, and for ingratitude there's no atonement. Sugriva doesn't argue. Everything I have, he says, I owe to Rama. I may have slipped. Who doesn't? But I'm his friend, and I'll follow him with my whole army. If I've failed through carelessness, forgive me. He owns the fault, doesn't drown in it, and moves to action, and Lakshmana softens at once. Come and see Rama, he says. Sugriva bows before Rama with joined palms, and Rama receives him with an embrace and sits him at his side. While they talk, the armies arrive: monkeys and bears past counting, from mountains and seashores and snowy peaks, until they seem to cover the earth. The Sanskrit word for what Rama gives is kshama: forgiveness, and patience, and also a name for the earth, the one who bears everything. The Bhagavad Gita lists kshama among the divine qualities a person can grow. And many Hindus practice it before they're even out of bed. A morning prayer to the earth goddess, Bhumi, asks her: forgive me for touching you with my feet. The word for forgive there comes from the same root. Ask for kshama every morning, and you start learning to give it, from the one who bears everything. It meets a life now in families: someone slips and owns it, and the one let down doesn't keep a ledger. Rama doesn't hold the lost weeks against him. And then he turns to the real question: where do we look first?
screen: `NO ATONEMENT FOR INGRATITUDE.` · `SUGRIVA: FORGIVE ME.` · `AN EMBRACE, AND ARMIES.` · `KSHAMA: FORGIVENESS, THE EARTH.` · then, large: `FORGIVE ME FOR TOUCHING YOU WITH MY FEET.`

segments.voice: Try the old morning gesture: touch the floor with your fingers, then your heart or forehead, asking the earth's pardon for walking on her. If you don't pray, simply touch the floor and say thank you. Now think of a small fault of yours that someone might still be holding, and own it plainly: yes, I did that. Then think of someone you could forgive, and let your hand rest open on your knee, palm up.
Lakshmana's warning. It ends in Sugriva's apology, Rama's embrace, and kshama, patient as the earth.
Your line: kshama: forgiveness, patient as the earth. A fault owned, and no ledger kept. See you tomorrow.

594.title: Sugriva's map of the world
594.hook: four armies, four directions, and a land Hindus still walk as pilgrims
594.carry: tirtha: holy crossings in every direction
594.howItsDone: Many places named in the Ramayana are still tirthas, pilgrimage places; the Char Dham, at India's four edges (Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka, Rameswaram), is a pilgrimage many Hindus hope to complete in a lifetime.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's warning ended in Sugriva's apology and kshama, forgiveness as patient as the earth.

The rains are over and the roads are open. Sugriva stands before an army gathered from every forest and mountain he rules, and he has almost nothing to hand it: a bundle of jewels, a name, and one direction. The chariot flew south. That's all anyone knows. Somewhere beyond the forests and rivers and seas is one woman, and no one has an address. Sugriva's answer is to split the army four ways, and to give each leader directions so detailed they fill whole chapters.
screen: `ONE WOMAN, SOMEWHERE.` → `A HUGE ARMY, NO ADDRESS.` → `SPLIT FOUR WAYS.`

segments.voice: Sugriva sends Vinata east, Sushena west, Shatabali north, and to the south, where Ravana flew, his best: Angada, with Hanuman and the old bear Jambavan. For each direction he names rivers, mountains, kingdoms and seas, and strange places at the edge of the world. Some names are real, the Ganga, the Yamuna, the Godavari; others belong to myth. How does he know all this? Sugriva later tells Rama: when Vali chased him, he fled everywhere, and saw the whole world while running for his life. His exile became his map. And there's a deadline: one month, or answer with your lives. Here the story touches something Hindus still do with their feet. Many of the rivers and mountains on Sugriva's lists are tirthas, holy places. Tirtha literally means a ford, a crossing place, and many teachers explain it this way: somewhere the line between this world and the divine is thin enough to cross. Pilgrimage, tirtha-yatra, is one of the oldest Hindu practices. There's even a famous circle of four, the Char Dham, the four abodes at India's edges: Badrinath in the north, Puri in the east, Dwarka in the west, and Rameswaram in the south, which tradition links to Rama's own worship of Shiva. Many Hindus hope to reach all four in a lifetime. Sugriva sends armies in four directions to find one person. Pilgrims walk in four directions toward God. It meets a life now: families plan India trips around a temple, and grandparents save for a yatra. And many read Sugriva's map this way: the roads you walked in hard years can become a map for someone else.
screen: `EAST, WEST, NORTH, AND SOUTH.` · `A MAP LEARNED BY RUNNING.` · `TIRTHA: A CROSSING PLACE.` · `THE CHAR DHAM.` · then, large: `HOLY GROUND IN EVERY DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: Feel the four directions around you: in front, behind, left and right. Breathe into each in turn. Before a puja, many Hindus invite the holy rivers, the Ganga and others, into a small pot of water, so a pilgrimage comes to them. Picture one holy place, or anywhere you once felt close to something greater, and breathe as if you stood there. Then rest in the middle of all four.
The search parties. Four armies, four directions, and a land full of tirthas, places to cross over.
Your line: tirtha: holy crossings in every direction. Four armies for Sita, four dhams for God. That's day five hundred ninety-four.

595.title: Rama's ring
595.hook: a ring with Rama's name, and why Hindus write that name a thousand times
595.carry: nama: the name carries the one it names
595.howItsDone: Nama japa, repeating a name of God, is among the most common Hindu practices, and many devotees write Rama's name in notebooks (likhita japa); in paintings and temple carvings, Hanuman is often shown kneeling before Sita and holding out Rama's ring.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four search parties set out in four directions, with one month to report. Tirtha: holy crossings in every direction.

Before the southern party leaves, Rama calls Hanuman aside. Of all the leaders and all the armies, it's Hanuman he picks out. Sugriva's confidence in him is obvious, and Rama has his own reasons, going back to that first conversation on Rishyamuka, the sentence with not one word wrong. He takes something small off his finger and holds it out. It's the kind of thing you'd give someone only if you were sure of them.
screen: `RAMA CALLS HANUMAN ASIDE.` → `SOMETHING SMALL, HELD OUT.`

segments.voice: It's a ring, engraved with Rama's name. Take this, Rama tells him, so that when you find her, she'll know you come from me, and won't be afraid. Hanuman will meet Sita as a stranger, a monkey in an enemy city. Words alone might not be believed. A ring with his name will be. Why Hanuman? Valmiki gives the reason: Sugriva is surest of him, and Rama sees his resolve. Hanuman takes the ring, raises it to his head with joined palms, and bows at Rama's feet. Then the month passes. The parties to the east, west and north search everything and come back on time with nothing. Now everyone is waiting on the south. Notice what Rama sends: not a letter, his name. In Hindu devotion that's no small detail. Nama, the divine name, is treated as carrying the one it names. Nama japa, repeating God's name, is one of the most common Hindu practices: on a mala of beads, in a bhajan, under the breath on a bus. Some devotees write it, filling notebooks page after page with Sri Rama, a practice called likhita japa, written repetition. And many devotees say that wherever Rama's name is sung, Hanuman is there, listening. In the story, a name on a ring will tell Sita she isn't forgotten. Many teachers read the chanting the same way: the name brings the one named close. That's how it meets a life now, in a grandmother's notebook, or Ram written at the top of a page. And the week, in one line: from the rains to the ring, a friendship forgotten, warned, forgiven, and now carried in a name.
screen: `A RING WITH RAMA'S NAME.` · `THREE PARTIES RETURN EMPTY.` · `NAMA JAPA: REPEATING THE NAME.` · `LIKHITA JAPA: WRITING IT.` · then, large: `THE NAME CARRIES THE ONE IT NAMES.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus repeat a name of God with the breath, sometimes on a mala of a hundred and eight beads. Try it now: breathe in, and on the out-breath say Ram silently, or another name you love. If you don't pray, use the name of someone who trusts you. When the mind wanders, let the name be the ring that brings you back.
Anguliya, a finger-ring: the one Rama gives Hanuman today, engraved with his name, so Sita will know he sent him.
Your line: nama: the name carries the one it names. One small ring, one name, a lot of hope. Day five hundred ninety-five, done.
